title: API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions
content:
API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions

Earlier this month Anthropic announced a generous new benefit for their Max and Team subscriptions: $100, $200, and $500 per month subscribers would get the equivalent quantity of (expiring) credits to use with the Anthropic API.

OpenAI have now launched pretty much exactly the same deal: if you have a $100, $200, or $500 subscription plan with them you now get that same quantity of credits to apply to one of your API organizations.

I maintain subscriptions with both companies, so this is great news for me! I may even ship some public-facing demos now that the credits are already covered by my existing subscriptions.

Tags: ai, openai, generative-ai, llms, anthropic, llm-pricing

title: Apple Drops App Store Commission by a Whopping 4 Percentage Points in Taiwan
content:
Apple Developer News:

Apple is making changes to the Taiwan storefront of the App Store, following discussions with the Taiwan Fair Trade Commission.

As of October 31, 2026, the commission rate for standard Apple In-App Purchase and paid app transactions will be 26% on the Taiwan storefront of the App Store on iOS and iPadOS. Currently, that rate is 30%.

Well there we go. The App Store in Taiwan — just like in Japan — is fixed.

 ★

title: Custom Voices With Qwen3-TTS
content:
With my kids I’m currently building a little dungeron crawler and we’re trying to learn a bit about game development along the way. However given that we live in the modern times of increasing capabilities we wanted to get a narrator and voice over.

But we also wanted it to not sound like everyone’s standard AI voices so I looked into what options there are on the table. After some investigation I narrowed down to using Qwen3-TTS which uses voice embeddings for custom voices.

With a bit of creativity you can also do more with those custom voices than appears initially. In case this is of interest to you, this post just covers what we learned and with some examples. You can probably point your agent to it and it can do something with it.

What Qwen Offers

Qwen3 is not the only TTS model in town, and it wans’t even my first choice. We initially used Kokoro. However Qwen3 supports voice cloning and we wanted to have it feel a bit more unique.

In practice it’s a bit tricker though. Qwen3 ships three kinds of models:

  • 1.7B-Base (and 0.6B): clones a voice from a few seconds of reference audio
  • 1.7B-CustomVoice: comes with nine built-in speakers and instructions
  • 1.7B-VoiceDesign: invents a voice from a text description

The base model clones either in context or from the speaker embedding alone but there is no documented way to clone a voice and direct it with instructions. That means unlike the custom voice and voice design models you cannot say “speak sad” or “whisper” with a cloned base model.

At present the official options for a custom voice are fine-tuning Base on a single speaker or to make a clip with VoiceDesign and clone it with Base. That is not all that bad, but it means instructions are gone.

Playing With It

For this blog post I took 28 seconds of me from my talk at PyAI Conf, cut between two pauses so that it starts and ends on a full sentence, and transcribed it with Whisper. The transcript is really only needed for baking but to compare against an already existing voice it’s useful to have it say the same thing as the original recording.

Note that a conference talk recording is not ideal but it works anyways. Which is also a good reminder that you really don’t need a particularly clean recording (or a very long one) to get a halfway convincing version of a person. Particularly when then presented to you on a low quality phone call, it won’t be very hard to trick your grandmother.

The first thing you can do is to blend that recording with another voice. For instance you can use VoiceDesign to make up a voice from a description. For this blog post the designed voice was created like this, with Qwen’s own Python package qwen-tts (pip install qwen-tts, I used 0.1.1), which the rest of the code in this post uses too:

import torch
from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel

kw = dict(device_map="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="sdpa")
design = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-VoiceDesign", **kw)
wavs, sr = design.generate_voice_design(
    text=open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), language="English",
    instruct="A man in his forties with a warm, natural, medium-low voice, speaking "
             "clearly and calmly at an easy conversational pace, like someone reading "
             "aloud to a friend.",
)

You can see how the two different voices behave, particularly when blended together:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Voice Embeddings

What Base takes from a recording when cloning from the embedding alone is a speaker embedding which is basically 2048 numbers out of a speaker encoder that was trained. The same voice gets similar numbers and different voices get different ones. Which btw, is also a convenient way to do speaker detection from recordings if you want to! It’s not perfect, but it’s quite helpful for a single audio track recording to tell two speakers apart if you do some basic slicing and dicing (more on that below).

Because it is just a vector, you can do arithmetic on it. For instance a weighted average of two embeddings is a spaker that is somewhere between two voices:

base = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base", **kw)

def fingerprint(path):
    prompt = base.create_voice_clone_prompt(ref_audio=path, x_vector_only_mode=True)
    return prompt[0].ref_spk_embedding

def blend(a, b, t):
    a, b = a.float(), b.float()
    mixed = (1 - t) * a + t * b
    return (mixed / mixed.norm() * ((1 - t) * a.norm() + t * b.norm())).to(torch.bfloat16)

armin, designed = fingerprint("voices/armin.flac"), fingerprint("voices/designed.flac")

Here is the same sentence in eleven blends:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Note that it stops sounding like me quite quickly, but it retains some of my features. And it for sure ends up with creating a unique voice regardless. I found some better successes when ensuing that the two voices have similar spectograms (eg: similar “recording setups”). In this recording you can hear that one voice picked up by the lapel mic was a bit hollow compared to the designed voice.

If you like a a voice that comes out, you can bake it back into a new recording that you can then use as reference:

import soundfile as sf

mixed = blend(armin, designed, 0.5)
audio, rate = say(open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), mixed)  # say() is shown further down
sf.write("voices/final.flac", audio, rate)
final = fingerprint("voices/final.flac")

The baked voice does not come back exactly as the blend but it makes handling it easier if you want to. It’s just one voice reference file.

So on the question of using those embeddings for speaker recognition: how good does that work? I took an episode of State of Agentic Coding, the podcast Ben and I record, cut it into 2-second windows one second apart and compared each with an embedding of me form the conference.

Somewhat surprising, but maybe not too surprising using my conference recording clip as the reference this does not work at all with Qwen3. If instead I take the 20 seconds where I introduce myself at the start of the episode as the reference, it gets 98% of the rest right.

On the other hand using a model that was trained for speaker verification instead does manage to pick me up from the conference recording clip. For instance ECAPA, finds me from the conference clip in 97% of the windows.

Here are 20 minutes of that podcast, classified by speaker with the different approaches:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Instructed Cloned Voices

But the embeddings a very useful for the voice cloning! But how to give them instructions? Base and CustomVoice manipulate the speaker the same way: one vector inserted into the talker’s input sequence. In CustomVoice that vector is a row of the embedding table. In Base it is the x-vector from the speaker encoder, which only Base has. The generation code takes either (voice_clone_prompt is a regular argument of generate), and the transformer weights of the two models are nearly identical. So take the embedding with Base, then hand it to CustomVoice instead of one of its speakers:

cv = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-CustomVoice", **kw)

def say(text, xvec, instruct=None, language="English"):
    ids = cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_assistant_text(text)])
    told = [cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_instruct_text(instruct)])[0]
            if instruct else None]
    voice = {"ref_code": [None], "ref_spk_embedding": [xvec],
             "x_vector_only_mode": [True], "icl_mode": [False]}
    codes, _ = cv.model.generate(
        input_ids=ids, instruct_ids=told, voice_clone_prompt=voice,
        languages=[language], non_streaming_mode=True,
        **cv._merge_generate_kwargs(temperature=0.7, subtalker_temperature=0.7),
    )
    wavs, rate = cv.model.speech_tokenizer.decode([{"audio_codes": codes[0]}])
    return wavs[0], rate

wav, rate = say("I really thought this would work.", armin,
                "Speak in a sad, sorrowful tone, voice low and heavy, on the verge of tears.")

Pick a speaker for the slot, a model and an instruction:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Instructions work on cloned voices, but less reliably than on the built-in speakers, and it depends on the emotion, but honestly, it came out better than I anticipated. Definitely good enough to have some true custom voices for a voice over that don’t necessarily sound like something, someone else has in their game.

Other Fun Math

If a voice is a point in a 2048-dimensional space and blending works we can maybe do some other funny math on it. The obvious one is to try to see if some math can be used to manipulate gender.

To find it I had VoiceDesign create 14 different voices for men and women each. When you then take the average woman minus the average man you can then move any voice along that direction:

women = torch.stack([fingerprint(f"design/f{i}.wav") for i in range(14)]).float()
men = torch.stack([fingerprint(f"design/m{i}.wav") for i in range(14)]).float()
middle = (women.mean(0) + men.mean(0)) / 2
axis = women.mean(0) - men.mean(0)
axis = axis / axis.norm()

def move(xvec, t):
    """Put the voice at position t along the gender axis, keep the rest."""
    x = xvec.float()
    return (x + (t - (x - middle) @ axis) * axis).to(torch.bfloat16)

Here is the result for my clone:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Anyways, that’s that. If you want to play around with Qwen3 TTS I hope this was of some help, and maybe you got some ideas of what to do with the voice embeddings. Use it for good, not evil.

title: Avoid Public Functions Calling Other Public Functions
content:
Avoid Public Functions Calling Other Public Functions

Oct 29, 2026

A small-scale rule of thumb. This article will land much better with a concrete example, but I am drawing a blank here, so you gotta just blindly trust my say so!

When implementing a software module, it’s often a case that you are writing a public function foo, and at least part of what foo does is already handled by another public function bar. The DRY instinct encourages you to call bar() from within foo. This usually creates problems down the line. Instead, create a new private function and refactor both foo and bar to call that shared helper:

Rationale: the goal of a public API is to provide an interface that works best at the call site. If parts of public API are re-used to implement the rest of the API, then there’s a tension between making the interface convenient for the outside user and making it convenient to use from within abstraction itself. Namely, functions tend to grow optional parameters that should never be set by the user. Crucially, the parameter growth and interface degradation can happen after the original code sharing.

By proactively making the shared implementation private, the tension is defused. You still might need to tinker with helper signature until it does everything it needs to do, but, because the helper is private, this is a cheap, local change.

A notable exception to this rule of thumb are “shortcut” APIs, where a public function is defined as a commonly used chain of calls to other public functions. There, the rule is the opposite — no private calls are allowed, to make sure that it is a genuine shortcut, and not a midlayer mistake.

P.S. While researching if anyone wrote a better blog post already, I stumbled upon a fun stack overflow question, asking, paraphrasing:

The most upvoted answer explains that it is indeed bad, because this makes mocking to test a single method in isolation more complicated. Which is, imo, a natural, but horrible consequence of misguided approach to testing. You shouldn’t be mocking your methods, you should mock your IO. And, similarly, you shouldn’t test methods, but rather software functionality (unless you are building a public library with a stable API, which is a fun and important, but very narrow fraction of software development).

The accepted answer says that this recommendation makes no sense if it is not backed by an industry wide or an organizational standard. Which somehow manages to make even less sense — you shouldn’t follow the guideline rules because they are written in sanctified ink! Rather, you should apply each particular rule because of the underlying reasons that motivate the rule. Guidelines and best practices articles can concentrate lots of good reasoning in a single place, but they don’t absolve you from thinking!

title: A New Kind of Chemistry
content:
Thanks to Kyle Schiller at Marathon Fusion for conversations and information that informed this essay. All errors are my own.

Much of modern civilization is built on top of chemical reactions, either to produce new materials (as in the blast furnace, which converts iron oxide into metallic iron), or to generate energy. Chemical reactions, as we’ve previously noted, work by rearranging how atoms hold their outermost electrons. Combine an atom of sodium and an atom of chlorine, for instance, and sodium’s outermost electron will end up in chlorine’s outer electron shell in an ionic bond, creating sodium chloride — common table salt.

With these sorts of chemical reactions, we’re only shifting around atoms and the electrons that orbit them in the form of chemical bonds. The interior of the atom — the atomic nucleus, which contains an atom’s protons and neutrons — remains unchanged. But if you create the right conditions, it’s possible to rearrange the interior of atoms as well. In nuclear fission, the reaction that powers nuclear power plants, the nucleus of an atom splits, creating several new atoms and releasing an enormous amount of energy in the process. In the fusion reaction taking place within the sun, hydrogen atoms are fused together, their individual nuclei combining to form helium. In particle accelerators like the Large Hadron Collider, charged particles are accelerated into each other using electromagnetic fields, and scientists study the various fragments created by the collisions.

By changing the number of protons or neutrons in the nucleus, these nuclear reactions can create things that can’t be created via conventional chemistry. Change the number of neutrons in an atom, and you get a new isotope of that particular element: an atomic variant of the same chemical, but with a different mass. Change the number of protons, and you end up with a different element entirely, possibly one that doesn’t occur in nature at all.

Typically, the products of these reactions (which we’ll simply refer to as “isotopes”) are unstable: they decay into some other, more stable isotope, emitting radiation in the process, which can be harnessed for various purposes. Carbon dating, for example, relies on the fact that living organisms absorb carbon-14, an isotope of carbon with eight neutrons in the nucleus that eventually and reliably decays into atomically stable nitrogen-14 (the “14” indicates the number of protons and neutrons — carbon-14 has six protons and eight neutrons, while nitrogen-14 has seven protons and seven neutrons). Another process, radiographic welding inspection, uses a variety of radioactive isotopes, such as iridium-192 and selenium-75, to emit gamma rays to inspect welds. Smoke detectors rely on americium-241, an isotope of the artificial element americium — radiation emitted by a small amount of americium causes an electric current to flow across a chamber, but if smoke enters the chamber, the flow of electricity is interrupted, triggering an alarm.

Currently, our use of isotopes is constrained by the fact that creating them is difficult and expensive. Gram for gram, isotopes are some of the most expensive materials on the planet. And the supply chains to produce them are often extremely fragile. Technetium-99m1, a widely used radioactive isotope for medical imaging, is produced through the decay of another radioactive isotope, molybdenum-99. Molybdenum-99, in turn, is produced in only a few nuclear reactors around the world;there was a worldwide shortage in 2024 when some of these reactors went offline for repairs. If isotopes could be manufactured more easily and more cheaply, it could open up numerous possibilities — cheaper medical treatments, better nuclear power sources, possibly even useful new materials.

Making isotopes

We’re all familiar with the periodic table, which lists every chemical element known to man.

Each element on the periodic table has an atomic number, which is the number of protons in the nucleus, starting from atomic number 1 (hydrogen, which has one proton in the nucleus) all the way up to atomic number 118 (oganesson, an artificial element with 118 protons in the nucleus). It’s the number of protons in an atom that makes an element an element — carbon always has six protons, because having six protons in the nucleus of an atom is what makes that atom carbon.

But there are also neutrons in the nucleus, and the number of neutrons can vary. Most carbon on Earth, for instance, is carbon-12, which has six protons and six neutrons. But about 1% of carbon is carbon-13, which has seven neutrons. The most common isotope of helium is helium-4, which has two neutrons, but there’s also helium-3, which only has one. Most of the water molecules in Earth’s oceans are made up of hydrogen with no neutrons (hydrogen-1), but about one out of every 3200 water molecules contains a hydrogen with one neutron, also known as deuterium (water made from deuterium is sometimes known as “heavy water”).

We can visualize isotopes on what’s called a nuclide chart, shown below. The horizontal axis is the number of neutrons in a nucleus, while the vertical axis is the number of protons.

We can see that most elements have several different isotopes, most of which are unstable. Only the isotopes in black in the chart above are stable; everything else will eventually decay. Red isotopes on the chart above decay by what’s known as “beta-plus” decay or electron capture, turning a proton into a neutron. Teal isotopes decay by “beta-minus” decay, turning a neutron into a proton. Yellow isotopes decay by “alpha” decay, emitting an alpha particle (two protons and two neutrons). The rate at which an isotope decays into another isotope is typically described as its “half-life” — the amount of time it takes for half of a sample to undergo radioactive decay. Half-lives can vary wildly, from tiny fractions of a second for hydrogen-5 to hundreds of millions of years for uranium-235.

For isotopes that are stable, or that decay slowly enough that they can be found in the environment, it’s sometimes possible to obtain them by separating them out from other isotopes. But this is often difficult, because isotopes tend to be chemically identical, and most separation methods must rely on minute differences in the atoms’ weights. Much of the difficulty in the Manhattan Project, for instance, was in creating sufficient concentrations of a specific isotope of uranium, uranium-235, that would undergo nuclear fission. Uranium-235 only makes up about 0.72% of natural uranium, and producing a single, football-sized lump of it required a processing facility the size of a small city.

But many isotopes can’t be found in nature at all. There’s no natural source of the technetium-99m or molybdenum-99 used for medical imaging, or the selenium-75 used for welding inspection. It’s thus useful to be able to manufacture specific isotopes.

How do we do this?

At a high level, creating isotopes means rearranging the interior of an atom. In some cases, this happens by natural radioactive decay. The americium-241 used in smoke detectors, for instance, mostly comes from decaying plutonium-241. But for most isotopes we’re interested in, we can’t rely on natural mechanisms; instead, we have to deliberately rearrange atomic nuclei by bombarding them with different sorts of particles. Depending on the sort of particle you hit the nucleus with, the energy of that particle, and the nature of the target atom, you can create different sorts of reactions. These reactions are typically described by the following format: target(input particle, released particle)product. So in 1917 when Rutherford bombarded nitrogen atoms with alpha particles, producing oxygen and hydrogen nuclei (protons), that reaction was N-14(alpha,p)O-17. The figure below shows different sorts of reactions and how they move an atom to a different location on the nuclide chart.

There are a few different ways we can hit an atom with a particle. One is to use a particle accelerator, such as the cyclotron, invented in 1929 by Ernest Lawrence (who would go on to win a Nobel Prize for his invention). The cyclotron uses powerful electromagnetic fields to accelerate charged particles along spiral paths. With his 27-inch particle accelerator, Lawrence could accelerate helium nuclei to roughly 1% of the speed of light.

It wasn’t long after Lawrence created his cyclotron that it began to be used to create various isotopes. Naturally occurring radium was already being used to treat cancer with radiation, and Lawrence hired personnel to investigate the potential of using cyclotron-created isotopes for medical and research purposes, such as radioactive phosphorus-32. Phosphorus-32, which has one more neutron than the stable phosphorus-31, was a promising research isotope because organisms naturally incorporate and accumulate phosphorus: if that phosphorus were radioactive, it would allow various metabolic pathways to be observed and possibly allow for highly targeted radiation treatments. Lawrence quickly found that demand for phosphorus-32 for experimental cancer treatments and biological research was “almost insatiable,” and by 1939 a dozen cancer patients had been treated with cyclotron-produced phosphorus-32.

Particle accelerators are still used to produce isotopes today. GE Healthcare, for instance, sells several different medical cyclotrons. The GE PETtrace 800 uses a beam of hydrogen or deuterium nuclei (protons or proton + neutron) to create isotopes such as oxygen-15, nitrogen-13, and fluorine-18, which are then used for medical imaging.

The downside of particle accelerators is that it’s hard to use them to produce a large volume of material efficiently. A medical accelerator costs in the single-digit millions (plus several more millions for the facility to house it) and can only produce about a dust-grain-sized speck of material every hour.

This is due largely to how particle accelerators work. They accelerate particles using electromagnetic fields and so only work on charged particles: electrons, protons, or positively charged atomic nuclei. With electrons, it’s apparently hard to get them to trigger nuclear reactions because they don’t feel the strong nuclear force — electron accelerators thus mostly work by firing the electron into another target and triggering the release of gamma rays, but most of this beam will end up as heat. Because protons or alpha particles are positively charged, they’ll be repelled by the positively charged nucleus of the target, similarly reducing conversion efficiency and creating a lot of heat that must be dealt with. When the PETTrace 800 uses protons to make fluorine-18 (which uses oxygen-18 as an input), only about 1 in 800 protons enters the oxygen nucleus.

Another way to create the necessary particle collisions is to use nuclear fission: unstable atomic nuclei splitting apart when struck by a neutron. There are a couple of ways to leverage this. One is to simply harvest the products nuclear fission naturally generates. Molybdenum-99, for instance, is naturally produced during the fission of uranium-235 and plutonium-239. Strontium-90 is similarly a byproduct of nuclear fission and is sometimes harvested from spent nuclear fuel.

You can also use nuclear fission as a particle source. The fission of uranium-235 releases neutrons, which can then be used to bombard various targets to produce isotopes. Cobalt-60, for instance, a widely used radiation source, is created by placing cobalt-59 in a fission reactor, causing some of the atoms to absorb a neutron via neutron capture.

Using nuclear fission as a source of radioactive isotopes began almost as soon as the first nuclear reactors were created. Long before the Atomic Energy Commission built the first nuclear power plants, it was shipping reactor-created isotopes across the country and around the world for medical and scientific research. By 1956, more than a year before the first US civilian power station at Shippingport came online, there were 50,000 isotope purchases per year from the AEC.

But there are also drawbacks to using fission as an isotope source. For one, fission reactors are highly regulated, and constructing them is difficult and expensive. For another, most of the neutrons produced by fission reactors aren’t particularly high-energy, and in power reactors they’re generally deliberately slowed down to increase the chances that they’ll strike an atom and continue the chain reaction. The average fission neutron is created around 1.5–2 million electron volts (MeV), moving at about 6.5% of the speed of light, but in power reactors they’re slowed down using a moderator to about 0.025 electron volts. And even without moderation, the relatively low energy of most fission neutrons means that many nuclear reaction rates will be slow, and other reactions are out of reach.

To create isotopes efficiently, what we’d like is some way to generate a lot of neutrons at much higher energies. This would make many sorts of nuclear reactions possible while avoiding the inefficiencies of using particle accelerators.

One way to do this is with nuclear fusion. Much has been made about the difficulties of creating a fusion power plant, but fusion has always been a problem of efficiency: getting more energy out of your reaction than you put into it. Creating the fusion reaction in the first place has never been the issue, and fusion reactions have been created in the lab as far back as the 1930s. And these fusion reactions reliably produce high-energy neutrons. While fission can produce high-energy neutrons, only around 0.1% of them will be above 10 MeV. By contrast, neutrons produced when fusing hydrogen-2 (deuterium) and hydrogen-3 (tritium) are 14 MeV or more. Fusion has historically not been used to produce isotopes, but today a variety of startups and organizations are pursuing the idea. SHINE Technologies is currently building a facility, Chrysalis, to create Mo-99 via a complex process that requires a particle accelerator, a fission reaction, and a fusion reaction. Italy’s SORGENTINA-RF program similarly wants to create Mo-99 using fusion-generated neutrons. Marathon Fusion wants to use fusion neutrons to create a variety of different isotopes, such as terbium-149 and actinium-225 for cancer treatments, as does New Zealand fusion startup OpenStar.

Possibilities of cheap isotopes

Beyond its ability to generate high-energy neutrons, fusion also has the potential to make isotope manufacturing dramatically cheaper, at least for some isotopes/reactions. Particle accelerators take a lot of energy to operate: GE’s PETtrace draws about 75 kW, roughly as much as 75 microwaves when it’s running, which sets some floor on how cheaply they can produce anything. At 75 kW, it would take around 0.7 terawatt-hours to produce a gram of fluorine-18, which is around 1.5 hours of the entire electricity output of the US.

Energy costs aren’t actually all that significant for medical isotope production, since the doses are microscopic (600,000 doses of fluorine-18 combined weigh about as much as a single grain of salt). But if you wanted to produce large amounts of isotopes — grams, pounds, tons — it would eventually become a binding factor. And a particle accelerator is essentially only producing isotopes: the isotopes must be priced high enough to recover the costs of building and operating the facility. With fusion, however, your isotope-producing reactions can (potentially) also produce energy — so if you use the right reactions, you could use the sale of that energy to help pay for the facility and its operation.2 It’s conceivable that the right energy-generating fusion reactions, in the right arrangements, might be able to produce isotopes far more cheaply.

What sort of things become possible if we can produce isotopes far more cheaply? There are a few major categories of interest.

Medicine

One of the largest isotope markets, with some of the most expensive isotopes, is medicine. With medical imaging isotopes, a patient is given a very small amount of radioactive material, which gets taken up by the body and (generally) incorporated into specific cells or substances. Fluorine-18, for instance, gets incorporated into a glucose-like molecule called FDG, that the body then absorbs as if it were glucose. By monitoring the radiation released by the isotope, some area of the body or biological process can be monitored.

Medical isotopes are also used for radiation treatment. Some elements naturally collect in certain areas of the body, and radioactive isotopes can be used to deliver targeted treatment. Iodine, for instance, naturally collects in the thyroid gland, and radioactive iodine-131 can be used to treat thyroid cancer. Other isotopes, such as actinium-225, decay by emitting alpha particles, which travel an extremely short distance in tissue, also making them useful for delivering very targeted radiation therapy. A better process for manufacturing these isotopes could potentially allow existing medical isotopes to be made more cheaply and reliably; actinium-225, for instance, is a potentially promising isotope for cancer treatment, but current supplies are so limited that only a small number of patients a year can be treated using it. A better process could also potentially enable the creation of entirely new medical isotopes.

Nuclear power inputs

Both fission and fusion reactors rely on isotopes for various parts of their operation. For fusion, the reaction that creates valuable tritium within the fusion cycle requires an isotope of lithium, lithium-6, which makes up about 7% of all lithium and which currently must be produced via an expensive process of lithium enrichment (which is currently only done in Russia and China). Conventional fission reactors, similarly, require the extremely pure lithium-7 produced by the same process, since naturally occurring lithium with too much lithium-6 would absorb too many neutrons. Some new proposed fission reactors, such as TerraPower’s molten salt reactor, require another isotope, chlorine-37, which is currently only produced by the gram but is needed by the ton. A reliable, cheap source of these sorts of isotopes could thus potentially be very valuable (though as I understand it these are much less valuable than medical isotopes, since they’re stable and can be produced via separation processes, so probably not something we’ll see produced via fusion in the near term).

Nuclear batteries

One of the many nuclear technologies that remain somewhat under-explored is nuclear batteries: a battery that generates electric current using a small amount of radioactive material. These sorts of batteries were used for pacemakers for several decades, and are used to power spacecraft, but with the ability to manufacture better battery isotopes many other uses might be found, such as undersea drones that can stay permanently submerged for monitoring undersea cables.

Materials

In some cases, the nuclear chemistry process might let you make “normal” materials that are otherwise difficult or expensive to get. Marathon Fusion got a lot of attention last year (and last week) for a fusion neutron-driven reaction that can create gold using mercury as an input.

Cheap nuclear chemistry might also allow you to more efficiently make what’s known as “isotopically pure” materials. Most elements found in nature have multiple stable isotopes, and thus any minerals or materials that contain them will contain a mix of different isotopes. Steel, for instance, will be a mixture of several different stable isotopes of iron (iron-54, 56, 57, and 58) and carbon (carbon-12 and 13). But if you could make isotopes very cheaply, you could possibly more easily produce materials entirely using one elemental isotope, such as semiconductors that only contain silicon-28.

In some cases, these isotopically pure materials might have interesting or useful material properties. Isotopically pure diamond has far higher thermal conductivity than regular diamond, for instance (as do, apparently, many other isotopically pure materials). And because of its different quantum-mechanical properties, isotopically pure silicon is useful for building quantum computers.

Historically producing isotopically pure materials has been so difficult that much about them remains unknown; reducing the cost of making isotopes could break open this field of study.

Conclusion

For many technologies, how big an impact they have is a function of how cheap they can get. Solar PV was a niche power generation technology before decades of falling down the learning curve; steel was an expensive material used in limited ways before Henry Bessemer and others found ways to produce it cheaply; Ford’s Model T changed the world not because it was the first car, but because of how cheaply Ford could manufacture it. So a technology that offers the potential to produce some existing thing far more cheaply is always interesting to me, and I’ll be paying attention to see how this develops with isotopes.

1

Technetium-99m is technetium that’s in what’s known as a “metastable” state, an excited state that eventually decays to regular technium-99, emitting gamma rays in the process.

2

Specifically, most fusion uses deuterium and tritium as inputs, known as D-T fusion. Deuterium is incredibly common, but tritium is rare and expensive. But you can add a step to the fusion reaction so that it also creates tritium, reducing or eliminating the need for an outside source of it.

title: Extremely brief history of PDP computers
content:
I don’t know why I started to put this together. These machines fascinate me, because so much of early computing/hacker type culture happened on them. I started writing a table, but realised a timeline would be more intuitive. In this graph, the price is for a minimal configuration and adjusted for inflation. The time is the memory cycle time, a decent proxy for speed.

Some notes:

  • The PDP-1 was created mostly as an experiment. At the time, industrial control systems used either humans or complicated contraptions of logic boards to make decisions. Some engineers at DEC wanted to see if there was a customer base willing to use general-purpose computers instead.
  • The PDP-4 was a variant of PDP-1 that was a little slower and much cheaper. It was not compatible with the PDP-1. The PDP-4 was upgraded with new chip technology and became the PDP-7, which was then optimised further for cost and speed and became the PDP-9.
  • The PDP-5 was created when they realised the PDP-1 and PDP-4 machines were overkill for industrial control systems. By being smaller, it could be much cheaper, at the cost of compatibility with PDP-1 and PDP-4. It was still intended for roughly the same market. The chip upgrade turned it into the PDP-8.
  • The PDP-6 was a completely different beast, aimed at a different market. It supported having tonnes of directly-addressable memory, as well as memory protection, so it could be used as a time-sharing system. The amount of memory made it run Lisp well. With the chip upgrade, it became the PDP-10.
  • The PDP-11 was a new architecture again, intended to subsume all the previous models, to avoid running three incompatible lines in parallel. There were many variants of the PDP-11, with various performance characteristics and corresponding price points. However, even its most powerful configuration wasn’t powerful enough to attract many PDP-10 users.
  • The VAX came much later, but it’s included in the table anyway because it is what eventually subsumed the PDP-10. The VAX was somewhat compatible with the PDP-11, but they served different markets.

(Continue reading the full article on the web.)

title: What I learned about power from LBJ and Robert Moses
content:
Thanks to Max Farrens, who paired with me in writing the script for this video essay.

I recently interviewed Robert Caro. He’s spent the last 50 years writing a four volume biography of Lyndon Johnson, and he spent another 7 years before that writing the biography of Robert Moses, the master builder of New York. His books are widely regarded as the best explorations of political power that have ever been written.

They also happen to be literally my favorite books ever. Whenever I meet somebody new, one of the first questions they ask me is, “Who is it that you most want to interview that you haven’t yet?” And for six years, I’ve answered the question the same way: Robert Caro.

I’ve spent so much time trying to make this interview happen: chasing his agent, calling his publisher, contacting the museums that have his archives, and even sending him handwritten letters.

I finally got to sit down with him, and I’m very happy with how it turned out. It’ll be out this Friday.

In the meantime, as I was preparing for the interview, and rereading these biographies, I wrote down the lessons they laid out about how to accumulate and use power.

Robert Moses

Robert Moses was the master builder of New York. He built more of the physical city than anyone before or since: the Triborough and Verrazano bridges, the Cross Bronx Expressway, Jones Beach, Lincoln Center, Shea Stadium, two giant power dams upstate, in addition to hundreds of parks and dozens of pools. Of the 899 miles of highways completed in New York State by 1964, Moses had built 672 of them. His projects collectively cost hundreds of billions of dollars in today’s money.

For more than 30 years, Robert Moses was the most powerful person in New York (more powerful than any elected mayor or governor, despite not being elected to anything). How did he get and keep that much power?

Exploits in law

Part of the answer is that Moses wrote the laws that governed him. He was called ‘the best bill drafter in Albany,’ and he used that skill to write himself powers that the legislators voting on his bills didn’t know they were granting.

The political genius of Robert Moses is perhaps best illustrated by his use of public authorities, which are government-created corporations that build city infrastructure. Public authorities sell bonds to pay for a specific project, say a new bridge. Once the bridge is built, the authority would charge drivers a toll until it had collected enough money to pay off its bonds. Then the authority would tear down the tollbooths, hand the bridge over to the city, and go out of existence.

At least, that was the idea. And that’s what Albany assumed would happen when the New York State Legislature approved the Triborough Bridge Authority Act of 1933, whose final version included - buried within pages and pages of legalese - a few seemingly minor alterations drafted by Robert Moses.

Section 1 clearly stated that the authority would dissolve once the bonds were paid off. And since the bonds could run at most 40 years (and the revenues from the bridge would pay back the initial cost far sooner), it seemed like the authority had a clear, built-in expiration date. However, in a subsection of Section 9, Moses added a single sentence that said the Authority could “from time to time” pay off its old bonds by issuing new ones. And those new ones could be “for any other corporate purpose.” So just before the original bonds were about to expire, the authority now had the right to issue a totally fresh 40 year note, for a potentially totally different use.

And what could the Authority build with all that money? The original act let it build two bridges and their “approaches.” Moses’ amendments also gave this authority the right to build “connecting” roads and “facilities not inconsistent with the use of the project”. These rights, when interpreted as creatively as Moses intended to, would allow Moses to alter most of the roads, parks, and housing in New York - for if a road connected to a road which connected to a road which connected to the bridge, or if a park lay along the road that connected to the road that connected to the road that connected to the bridge, surely the Triborough Authority was entitled to improve and change it.

All this construction could be financed by the bridges’ enormous toll revenues and the right of the Triborough Authority to borrow against them. To give some perspective, in 1946, the entire New York City government could only borrow $150 million before hitting its legal debt limit. That very same year, Triborough could borrow $360 million. So Moses’ bridge authority had access to more than double the amount of money as the largest city in America.

But what if a future governor or mayor eventually learned about all the power and revenue that had been delegated to this authority, and decided to claw back? Moses had planned for that too, and his solution was so clever that no lawyer or lawmaker in Albany saw it coming. The US Constitution says that no state shall make “any … Law impairing the Obligation of Contracts” entered into by a government entity. A bond issued by a public authority is such a contract. Moses snuck a clause into the law that allowed him to add into those bond contracts “any other matters, of like or different character, which in any way affect the security or protection of the bonds”. These “matters” included whether Triborough could charge tolls for however long they wanted, and whether they would get to keep the surplus thus generated.

That is to say, Moses could now entrench his powers simply by writing them into the bonds he issued. From the moment the bonds were sold, those powers could no longer be revoked by the Legislature, the governor, or the mayor - by anything, in fact, short of a Constitutional Convention. The powers that Moses now had were guaranteed for the bonds’ entire lifetime - a lifetime which could always be extended simply by refinancing.

So, with just a few minor tweaks, Moses turned an act meant to allow the construction of two bridges into the basis of an institution that could build basically anything it wanted anywhere in New York (and whose authority to do so was protected by the U.S. Constitution).

The indispensable man

These bond covenants had turned Triborough Authorities’ power into granite, but nothing in them guaranteed that Robert Moses would remain as chairman. So how did Moses retain his position for 30 years?

Part of the answer is, again, the law. Moses drafted the Triborough act so that its commissioners could be removed mid-term only “on stated charges after a formal hearing.” But any differences he had with a mayor or governor were more about what he decided to build and whom he displaced to build it, rather than personal conduct.

As Caro says, “Robert Moses was not himself corrupt. He was, in fact, as uninterested in obtaining payoffs for himself as any public servant who ever lived. In the politicians’ phrase, he was ‘money honest.’”

So, there were never any formal charges to bring. But this only explains why he wasn’t fired in the middle of his term. Why was he reappointed every six years? Well, at his peak, Moses was a hydra with a dozen heads. He held 12 different government posts at the same time: city construction coordinator, chairman of the State Council of Parks, chairman of the State Power Authority, and so on. Some of these positions were appointed by the mayor, some by the governor, so no single person could cut off all his heads simultaneously. And removing him from any one position meant making an enemy of the man who would still be the most powerful person in New York.

More importantly, no mayor or governor wanted to fire him. The way we remember Robert Moses today is based on a reputation that calcified in the 1970s, when The Power Broker came out and New York was experiencing a dark age of crime, deindustrialization, and white flight. Moses got much of the blame (the subtitle of The Power Broker is “Robert Moses and the Fall of New York”). In my opinion, that crisis had more to do with large structural factors than with Moses himself - cities he had nothing to do with, like Detroit and St. Louis, experienced a much more dramatic collapse.

For the vast majority of his career, Moses was incredibly popular. In the 1930s and 1940s, New York high schools voted Moses ‘the most admired New Yorker’. This was because he had delivered, over and over again, public works which millions of New Yorkers got to use and enjoy: beaches, parks, pools, and playgrounds, as well as the bridges and the parkways that let families drive out to them. And he did so at a speed and a scale that nobody had seen before: in just his first four months as the city’s Park Commissioner, by keeping crews working around the clock, he finished 1,700 park renovations. And he did it all without a whiff of personal scandal.

As Caro writes in The Power Broker, “[I]t was not unusual at park and playground opening ceremonies for children, prodded by their parents, to break into the cheer ‘Two, four, six, eight—who do we appreciate? Mr. Moses! MR. MOSES!! MR. MOSES!!!’”

Importantly, Moses could deliver these enormous and popular public works within a timeframe that fit into a single election cycle. If a mayor gave Robert Moses the power to build something, he could expect to be standing at the ribbon-cutting for it before he was up for re-election. Today, it’s almost unimaginable that the government could construct something big in a year or two. For example, construction on the Second Avenue subway in New York began in 1972; the first section was opened in 2017, and just these initial 2 miles cost taxpayers $4.5 billion.

A lot of the funding for public works comes from Washington - cities that receive the most money are the ones who have already finalized their blueprints and can break ground as soon as a new federal initiative is announced. Moses had the largest and best team of planners and engineers in the country. And because of that, by 1936, New York was getting one-seventh of the money that the federal government had set aside for Depression era work-relief… for the entire nation. And the projects this funding was going towards were the ones chosen by Moses. If the mayor had some different idea about what should be constructed, he’d have to draw up his own plans, which he didn’t have the independent technical expertise to do. So he could either build the projects that Moses wanted to build or build nothing at all.

Between his popularity, his unique ability to get things done, and his control over money, Moses had a lot of leverage. And he was not shy about using it. Far from being worried about getting fired, Moses would constantly threaten to quit whenever he didn’t get his way. Under Mayor Wagner, one aide said, “it seemed like he was resigning about one thing or another about twice a day.” He threatened resignation to La Guardia so often, over such small things, that La Guardia’s lawyer got a stack of forms printed that read “I, Robert Moses, do hereby resign as…”, to save Moses the trouble of writing it out every time.

Behind that joke was real fear. If a mayor accepted that resignation, not only would he be forfeiting completion of whatever projects Moses was working on (along with the money apportioned for those projects), he’d also be picking a public fight with the most respected official in all of New York. Moses had spent years befriending the owners of the city’s newspapers - he spent weekends at the summer home of the Sulzbergers, the family that owned the New York Times. The mayor knew that if Moses resigned, the next morning, all the front pages would tell the story of how the man above politics was driven out by a craven politician because he refused to compromise the city’s interests.

The coalition for yes

And the power that Moses derived from his popularity with the masses was nothing compared to the power he derived from his connections with New York’s powerful private interests.

We are very used today to NIMBY, where powerful but concentrated interest groups manage to stymie projects despite their broad popularity. Moses built a concentrated faction for YIMBY. He built a graft machine that greased the wheels for new construction, because it ensured the most influential people in the state would all benefit whenever a project got underway.

The banks got to buy his bonds at a steep discount without competitive bidding, the unions got more jobs, politically connected lawyers got legal fees, and party bosses got paid to broker insurance policies on bridges that had no plausible risk of falling down. Moses could then rely on these beneficiaries to call up anyone who stood in the way of one of his projects, whether that was a borough president or the governor himself.

Power reveals

Caro paints Moses as someone who began as an idealist, rather than someone who craved power from the start. In the 1910s, Moses was a brilliant young reformer who joined this new “good government” movement, which was trying to replace Tammany Hall’s patronage with honest and competent administration. He spent years fighting the machine. But his reforms got killed - the machine won. Moses learned that ideals are useless without the power to realize them. Caro writes:

In the beginning—and for decades of his career—the power Robert Moses amassed was the servant of his dreams, amassed for their sake, so that his gigantic city-shaping visions could become reality. But power is not an instrument that its possessor can use with impunity. It is a drug that creates in the user a need for larger and larger dosages. And Moses was a user.

Lyndon Johnson’s story, on the other hand, is kind of the opposite. For most of his career, there was little evidence he had a coherent political ideology - he was a ruthless power-seeker who embraced whatever happened to be most expedient at the time. When Johnson first entered the U.S. Senate, he realized that the most powerful men there were conservative Southern Dixiecrats. And the Johnson that they encountered was one who had molded himself to their form.

While writing Master of the Senate, Caro interviewed former Georgia Senator Herman Talmadge. He asked Talmadge what impression he got from freshman Senator Lyndon Johnson about the proper relationship between white people and black people.

“Master and servant.” So I [Caro] asked, Well didn’t Johnson have any sympathy for blacks, any desire to improve their lot? My notes say “long pause.” And then I wrote [Talmadge’s] two-word reply: “None indicated.” Another pause, and then: “He was with us in his heart. I believed him. I believed him.”

Of course, we know that once he became president, Johnson spearheaded the 1964 Civil Rights Act and the 1965 Voting Rights Act, the most important civil rights laws since Reconstruction.

So Moses began as a naive idealist but, in Caro’s telling, became someone seeking power for its own sake. Johnson was an ambitious opportunist from the very start, and it was only once he had real power that he used it for ideals few knew he had.

Lyndon Johnson

Lyndon Johnson was the most powerful Senate majority leader - perhaps the most powerful legislator period - in the history of this country. Here’s Caro in Master of the Senate:

He was master of the Senate—master of an institution that had never before had a master, and that at the time, almost half a century later, when this book is being written, has not had one since.

No leader before Johnson had wielded this kind of power, because the Senate had been deliberately set up by the founders to not be “led”. When Johnson asked the Library of Congress for a list of the Majority Leader’s formal powers, he found that there was only one: the right to be recognized first on the floor. Before Johnson, the Majority Leader was less a leader and more a lightning rod. He’d be blamed in the national press and in his home state for everything the Senate failed to do, yet he had no actual power to do anything about those failures. Being in this predicament was so politically toxic that Johnson’s two predecessors as majority leaders had both lost their own Senate seats.

A big part of the reason that Johnson became his party’s leader at just 44, in a Senate whose average age was around 60, was that hardly anyone else wanted such a thankless and useless job. And in their hands, this job would have remained useless. But they were not Lyndon Johnson.

Johnson turned himself into the second most powerful man in America (right behind the president) in three different ways.

Things to promise, things to threaten with

Johnson transformed the Senate’s rules, institutions and norms so that he alone had the power to grant important favors to his colleagues. If a senator needed a bill passed, Johnson was the one who could get it scheduled on the floor and persuade the committee chairman to report it out. If the bill needed help in the House, Johnson was the one with a direct line to Speaker Sam Rayburn. And if the senator needed money for his next campaign (to ensure that he would remain a senator), Johnson was the one who could put in a good word with oilmen from his native Texas.

Johnson also put himself in a position to control committee assignments, which are the single biggest factor that shapes how a senator’s whole career plays out. For about a century, they had been handed out by seniority. Practically overnight, Johnson changed the system so that many seats were no longer being settled by seniority but rather negotiated by the party’s Steering committee, which Johnson controlled. If you wanted a good seat, you had to do what Johnson wanted. In 1957, Estes Kefauver voted against Johnson on an important motion. That very same week, the highly coveted open seat on the Foreign Relations Committee, which Kefauver was expecting to get, was instead handed over to a far more junior senator named John F. Kennedy.

The real political genius of Lyndon Johnson was identifying and then gaining control over every possible source of leverage over his colleagues. Whatever a senator needed to survive, whether that was money, committee seats, or the passage of bills that matter to his home state, Johnson could give, and Johnson could withhold.

Setting the agenda

What the final bill that passes says depends on which one version actually comes to a vote, and with what final modifications. Whoever gets to set the agenda controls the outcome. So you won’t be surprised by who put himself in this position. Johnson’s main tool for setting the agenda was the unanimous consent agreement. By default, Senate debate is unlimited. A senator can talk about a bill for as long as he likes, and as he does so, he can also offer amendments that have nothing to do with that bill, each of which can stall the bill even further. A unanimous consent agreement sets those freedoms aside for a single bill: it fixes the allotted time for debate and constrains the opportunity to amend it. Earlier leaders rarely used such agreements, and even then, only after weeks of debate on a bill had already exhausted all the senators. Johnson made their use the norm in the Senate. He wouldn’t even allow a bill to reach the floor until such an agreement was in place.

Johnson wanted to control which bill reached the floor, and to keep the floor from changing anyone’s mind, because he wanted every vote settled in private beforehand, through the wheeling-and-dealing where his leverage worked best. The last thing he wanted was for a long, public debate on the merits of the bill to change a senator’s mind at the last minute, or for a surprise amendment to unravel a deal he had spent weeks painstakingly brokering. As Paul Douglas put it, under Johnson “all the action takes place offstage, before the play begins.”

The view from the center

Johnson made sure that as much of the Senate’s information as possible ran through him. He had every committee assign a staffer to tell him what was being drafted. His aides tracked what every senator was up to. And he spent his own days in the cloakroom and the hallways cajoling and listening to his colleagues. So he knew what each senator really wanted, what he would and wouldn’t give up to get it.

In any session, the Senate faces hundreds of possible bills and amendments. A senator’s vote on one bill can be traded for another senator’s vote on a different one, and any single bill can be amended a dozen ways to win someone over. So there’s an almost endless combination of possible deals to be made. Johnson made sure that he was the one instigating and brokering most of these deals. As a result, he could make sure that any deal left Johnson coming out ahead.

A good example here is how he got the Civil Rights Act of 1957 passed through the Senate. Johnson was desperate to make sure that a civil rights bill passed that year, even if it was weak. That’s because he wanted to be president, but no Southerner with his record of consistently voting against civil rights could hope to win the Democratic presidential nomination in 1960.

The problem was that there seemed to be no bill strong enough to win Northern liberals yet weak enough that the Southerners wouldn’t filibuster it. The sticking point was who would preside over the court cases where Southern electoral officials were accused of suppressing black voters. Southern Senators insisted on jury trials. But Northern Senators were livid - this would gut the whole bill. The entire point of the law was to combat the exclusion of black citizens from the voting rolls, but Southern states required jurors to be registered voters. An all-white Southern jury would never convict white registrars for turning away black voters.

Any version that one side could accept, the other would reject. A less creative legislator would have backed one side or fallen into the chasm between the two. But over the course of seven months, Johnson built a masterful deal that brought together wholly unrelated factions, and whose byproduct included the passage of this civil rights law. Western senators got a federal dam they had wanted for years between Idaho and Oregon. Midwestern Republicans, who had powerful railroad unions in their state, got the right to a jury trial extended to striking workers. And moderates got a clause guaranteeing that black citizens could serve on federal juries, so they could tell voters they had created a new civil right. Meanwhile the jury-trial guarantee for Southern registrars stayed in, which kept the bill weak enough that the Southerners agreed not to filibuster.

A dam in Idaho, protections for union workers, and federal jury rules had nothing to do with voting rights in the South. At least, not to anyone who lacked the shrewd inside understanding and political creativity of Lyndon Johnson.

Coda

Caro’s books are the best-written accounts of how political power actually works. But they are written so compellingly, with characters more vivid and stories more gripping than any novel, that it’s very easy to get so engrossed that you just keep turning the pages. And you never step back to ask what lessons the stories teach about power.

I wanted to write this essay, both so that I could think through what those lessons actually are, and also so that you would have the context necessary to watch my interview with Caro and get as much out of it as I did when I spoke to him.

You’ll be able to watch the interview this Thursday. By the time you’re reading this, it might be already out. I hope you enjoy it!

title: Celebrating SIM Cards
content:
It’s time to celebrate a little win.

The other day, my mom contacted me saying her 10-year-old iPhone wouldn’t turn on.

After getting a hold of the device and doing some family IT support, I concluded the battery was dead.

So I bought her a new (old) one on Walmart (SE 3rd gen., if you must know).

Her old phone used a SIM card, so I was expecting the process to go something like this:

  1. Take the SIM out of the old phone
  2. Put it in the new phone
  3. Setup the device
  4. Troubleshoot why there was no service
  5. Call my Mom’s carrier and work through the issue

But step 4 and 5 never happened.

The new phone “just” connected. I called her number. I texted it. Everything worked as expected.

Everything worked as expected.

Everything worked as expected.

I didn’t have to Google a single question.

I was floored.

Flabbergasted.

I know I shouldn’t have been because that’s how SIM cards are supposed to work, right? Like that’s the whole promise of a SIM card: you can seamlessly swap them between phones.

And in this case, the tech worked exactly as promised.

As I write this, I’m kind of amazed at how amazed I am that everything “just worked”.

Shout out to anyone who has ever worked on SIM card technology.

More things like this please :)

title: Making agents fast - what I've learnt over the last 12 months
content:
I've spent a lot of my career optimising websites and apps to run faster, and it's been interesting to apply some of those principles to agentic workflows. I'll run over some of my key learnings - there's many more I want to get written down at some point, but for brevity I think this is my rough mental model of tackling this.

Inference speed

The obvious thing to start with is inference speed. This has two key components, which will be familiar if you have done any backend API optimisation.

The first is TTFT (time to first token). This is analogous to TTFB (time to first byte) in web servers, namely how quickly does the first token come after you've done a request. This includes prefill (input token processing), so this scales with how many tokens the agent is sending to the inference provider too - so you should expect to see (potentially significant) variance on this number, much like you'd expect TTFB to be higher on an endpoint that e.g. has to do more database calls to prepare the response. A lower TTFT is better.

Prompt caching is, of course, absolutely vital to this. Cached tokens are much faster (and cheaper!) to serve. Most agent harnesses handle this well these days - it's been a while since I've ever seen issues with this. Obviously worth keeping an eye on, but it matters less than I predicted in real world experience.

The second is tok/s (tokens per second), which measures how quickly tokens come back once the response starts. This is closer to bandwidth on application servers, where a higher value is better.

How relatively important each are depends on what kind of responses you're expecting back from the LLM provider. For example, if you are sending back and forth lots of short responses between turns in your agentic workflow, TTFT is likely to comparatively be of greater importance than tok/s. Equally, if you are having the LLM output longer responses (say, code or documents), then TTFT is likely to be less important than tok/s.

Illustrative numbers. TTFT is network, queueing and prefill - the wait before anything comes back. Tok/s is how fast it streams once it starts.

Knowing which number you need faster is important when comparing models and inference providers. Smaller models are generally faster than big ones. But between providers of the same model[1], there is an enormous delta in speed. OpenRouter does provide public data on inference providers, but keep in mind this is an aggregate that may only roughly match your real world use.

The main issue that tends to crop up is that providers also tend to vary in speed a lot depending on the time of day and how much load they are under. Big leaps in TTFT (for similar length prompts) can indicate queuing on the provider side, but can also mean your requests are being allocated to slower hardware or more users competing for prefill compute. Equally, slowdowns in tok/s can mean slower underlying hardware or higher batch sizes at the provider. Either way, there is a serious "noisy neighbour"[2] factor on many inference providers.

Of course, many providers offer different tiers of service. For example, OpenAI offers a 'flex' tier alongside their standard and 'fast' tiers. These allow you to trade speed for cost.

But don't overlook the impact of thinking budgets. A "fast" tier model with thinking set to maximum or xhigh will be vastly slower than a "slow" tier model with low or medium thinking. I'm guilty of constantly overlooking thinking budgets when looking at this stuff, but it makes an enormous difference. It's easy to be drawn to the quantitative tok/s and TTFT values when in reality reducing thinking can completely dwarf it - if suitable for your task.

But it's not all about inference speed

While having fast(er) inference never hurts, it's worth noting that it's often not the biggest part of the speeding up agents, and can be expensive to speed up (paying for faster tiers), or painful to move inference providers (if you have committed spend or contractual requirements).

Rough numbers again, but halving inference time only takes 20% off the task when provisioning, tools and suspend/resume stay the same.

It's good to start looking at your tool calls in more detail. This is much more classic performance optimisation work. But I've noticed things being slow that are not usually slow. A classic example is an agent running xargs -I{} over large amounts of files, which causes hundreds of thousands of new process invocations. This can be painfully slow, especially on sandboxed environments.

So while classic software performance engineering applies as per normal to agent tool calls, you need to investigate tool call traces to see what the agent does. It will often chain a bunch of bash commands together to achieve a result and it can be not obvious to see which part is causing slowness. strace is helpful here, but not ideal to run all the time as it itself has a performance overhead.

Tool output size matters too. While most agent harnesses are pretty strict at stopping cat-style commands from blowing up your context window, as mentioned before uncached input tokens directly impact TTFT. SQL-style data sources have a big advantage if you can give your agent access to these - as it can request exactly what it needs without risk of a broad awk returning thousands of tokens of unrequired data.

Equally, given many agents start a new shell on every command things in your .bashrc that are not usually an issue can become a real issue. Be careful about what a shell needs to launch - especially if you have nvm or similar in that. Before you know it you can be spending dramatically more time starting the shell than running the command.

Build the tooling your agent wants

Building on from the obvious "make this command faster", I think the next step is to think hard about what tooling your agent needs, but is having to "work around". For example, if you have it doing a lot of xargs over markdown files over and over, it is potentially better for that data to be in a database it can call with full text search.

This is where things differ a little in my mental model of software optimisation. Usually you look at a request, look at what it's doing, and try and make each part faster, and rinse and repeat. With agentic workflows, you can often just observe what the agent does, and deduce what would work better. So purely looking at tool call traces can be misleading.

I've found that open weights models have a massive advantage here as you can read their thinking traces. While CoT traces are well used by the labs trying to work on safety and alignment, it turns out they are great for coming up with ideas to optimise the tools you give the agent.

The way I've worked with this is getting a list of slow calls, and looking at the thinking blocks just before this. You'll usually get some blindingly obvious "hmm, could do x, but no y" style thoughts. And you can just give the agent what it wants, and see how things work out.

The other thing that can make a big difference is treating for loops with sleep as a red flag. This is an indication that the agent wants to be notified of something but is instead having to poll for it. Often agents will poll for something that is quick but they tend to set a 10 or 20s minimum wait on the for loop. This can be solved with prompting sometimes, but often it can be an indication that (usually external) services need a async way to fire back task completion.

Finally, parallelisation is a big help in cutting down speed of tool execution. Adding a simple "try and parallelise tool calls in $TASK" can work wonders, but especially with weaker models risks the agent making mistakes and undoing any efficiency gain. As such, providing tools (CLI or MCP) that do the parallel steps for the agent can be worthwhile.

A quick hardware reminder

In my career, primarily driven by cloud computing platforms, I've often found the easiest quick fix is to just use faster hardware. And by faster hardware I do not mean a bigger AWS instance - dig into the underlying hardware your agents are running on. That means looking at the exact CPU core type you are using (the Zen 4c/5c cores can be much slower than the full sized ones), clock frequency and file IO speeds.

This depends heavily on the tasks you're doing with your agents, but if they need to write a lot of custom code or doing a lot of data analysis, making sure the underlying hardware is fast can help a lot.

For example, if your agent needs to do quite IO-heavy tasks, you may find a lot of your slowness is coming from networked disks. Having faster (local) NVMe disks may offer many, many orders of magnitude faster IO performance.

This is often worse in many sandboxes. With things like copy on write and other snapshotting techniques, there can be a lot of overhead on file IO. Slow underlying IO just makes everything worse.

Suspend and resume

I often see real speed issues with suspend and resume. Not every agentic workflow uses it, but if you (for example) allow agents to pause for a human in the loop approval, you need to be careful with optimising suspend and resume.

MicroVMs can often resume on paper extremely quickly, but actually have pages streamed in on first access. So you need to measure not just what the MicroVM says but how quickly new inference requests are starting after resume.

Being careful with memory management is the crucial thing here. While you don't want to starve your VMs of RAM and thus cause swap or OOMs, it's worth investigating what is using RAM during a suspend. If you have for example headless browser sessions active, it's almost certainly worth killing them before suspending, as is any running server processes the agent may have built.

As always, the key thing is to measure and track RAM usage and break it down over time if you are using a lot of suspend/resume cycles.

Finally, check the network. It's very common in my experience to have broken IPv6 in sandbox environments, and you end up with network timeouts while it does a AAAA lookup on DNS, which adds a small overhead to every request. Basic hygiene stuff like this adds up over the course of an agentic session.

Key takeaways

I think the key things I'd check on any agentic optimisation project are:

  • Inference speed is nuanced, and knowing what part of inference you rely on most for speed is important.
  • Check thinking budgets! This is overwhelmingly the lowest hanging fruit
  • Read traces, and if you are using open weight models read the CoT thinking traces. They often have so much valuable insight into what the agent is wanting to do
  • Give the agent the tools it wants rather than what you think it needs
  • Don't overlook the basic stuff. Faster hardware still matters, sandboxing and microVMs open a whole world of potential performance footguns, parallelisation helps and classic software performance optimisation is as relevant as ever.

As always, this space is also evolving fast. Keeping up to date with the field has always been my guiding north star in making sure you can keep stuff fast.

I'd love to hear from you if you're working on making agents faster. I'm especially interested if you think I'm missing obvious factors here!

  1. Be aware that even the same model may have different quantisation (compression) depending on the provider. You need to compare apples to apples - if one provider serves FP8 and another INT4 (say), it will be faster but at the cost of quality. ↩︎

  2. Noisy neighbour refers to shared compute getting slower when other users of the same hardware are pulling more resources. Typically you'd see this on VM providers with shared CPU resource - it may be fast a lot of the time, but when other customers are running high-load tasks, the hypervisor starts throttling each user. Unlike on VMs, where you can usually see this with vmstat's steal column, it's very opaque at what load your inference provider is under. ↩︎
